issues.legal_issue: A stipulation to pay rent can create a tenancy despite the cheque tendered for rent being returned unpaid, if exclusive possession is also established.
material_facts: A receipt recited that a cheque for Rs. 18,000 was given as rent for the premises for a twelve-month period.
The High Court construed the receipt as showing that a lease was intended, and the Supreme Court rejected the contention that the returned cheque negated the tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The stipulation to pay rent was sufficient consideration for a tenancy when exclusive possession was established; the cheque’s return did not negate the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 8 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a promise to pay rent may constitute consideration; actual non-payment is not equivalent to absence of consideration in law. A stipulation for rent, together with exclusive possession, can create a tenancy. The Court also relied on the principle that construction of a document forming the foundation of the parties’ rights raises a question of law.

rule.if: lease_status_dispute and receipt_stipulates_rent and exclusive_possession and rent_cheque_returned

predicates.lease_status_dispute: The parties dispute whether their arrangement created a tenancy.
predicates.receipt_stipulates_rent: A receipt or other document records a promise to pay rent for the premises.
predicates.exclusive_possession: The proposed tenant has exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.rent_cheque_returned: A cheque tendered for the promised rent is returned unpaid.

issues.definition: When a tenancy is disputed, a recorded promise to pay rent combined with exclusive possession establishes a tenancy even if the rent cheque is returned unpaid.

issues.legal_issue: Construction of a document that forms the foundation of the parties’ rights, and an inference drawn by applying legal principles to admitted or found facts, raise questions of law rather than questions of fact alone.
material_facts: The receipt was relied on to determine whether an earlier tenancy existed.
The High Court interpreted the receipt and inferred from it that a lease was intended.
The landlords argued that the High Court had impermissibly reappreciated facts in a second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s construction of the receipt raised a question of law, and the inference drawn by applying legal principles to the facts was a mixed question of fact and law; the challenge that it had entered forbidden factual territory was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The construction of a document forming the foundation of the parties’ rights raises a question of law. An inference from admitted or found facts is a question of law when it depends on applying proper legal principles, and the determination is then a mixed question of fact and law.

predicates.second_appeal_limited_to_law_questions: The proceeding is a second appeal in which review is limited to questions of law.
predicates.rights_based_on_document: The parties’ rights depend on a particular document.
predicates.document_requires_construction: The meaning or effect of that document must be determined to resolve the dispute.

issues.definition: In a second appeal limited to questions of law, construction of a document on which the parties’ rights depend raises a question of law.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a question of law is substantial depends on the circumstances, and a question already settled by the highest court is not substantial merely because it may be important, difficult, or consequential to a party.
material_facts: The landlords challenged the High Court’s jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground that the matter did not involve a substantial question of law.

The Court considered the meaning of a substantial question of law and relied on earlier decisions, including Raghunath Prasad v. Deputy Commissioner of Partabgarh, Sir Chunilal V. Mehta and Sons Ltd. v. The Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and Union of India v. M/s. Chaman Lal & Co.
issues.conclusion: The substantiality of a question of law depends on the facts and circumstances of the case; a question settled by the highest court is not substantial merely because it was once important or difficult or has a significant effect on a party.
issues.legal_principle: For an appeal requiring a substantial question of law, substantiality is assessed in light of the case’s facts and circumstances. A question already settled by the highest court does not remain substantial solely because of its past importance or difficulty, or its impact on a party. The Court relied on Raghunath Prasad v. Deputy Commissioner of Partabgarh, Sir Chunilal V. Mehta and Sons Ltd. v. The Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and Union of India v. M/s. Chaman Lal & Co.

predicates.second_appeal_requires_substantial_law_q: The proceeding is an appeal that may be brought only on a substantial question of law.
predicates.question_of_law_already_settled: The legal question has already been settled by the highest court.

issues.definition: In an appeal requiring a substantial question of law, a legal question already settled by the highest court is not substantial merely because of its importance, difficulty, or effect on a party.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot ordinarily use a collateral challenge in enforcement proceedings to invalidate a permission that has presumptive legal existence when the challenge disputes facts requiring investigation rather than showing an inherent lack of jurisdiction or an apparent nullity.
material_facts: The parties jointly applied to the Rent Controller and obtained permission for a limited tenancy under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
After the limited period expired without surrender of possession, the landlords sought possession through enforcement proceedings.
The occupants argued that the permission was vitiated by fraud because they had allegedly already been tenants and the premises were not available for letting on the relevant terms.

The permission was granted by the competent Rent Controller on the parties’ application; the challenge concerned the existence of underlying facts and required investigation, rather than an apparent absence of inherent jurisdiction.

The High Court treated the permission as a nullity that could be challenged collaterally, but the Supreme Court held that the permission had to be presumed valid until set aside in appropriate proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The permission could not be invalidated through the collateral challenge raised in the possession proceedings. A decision with presumptive existence and validity must be challenged by the proper person in proper proceedings at the proper time; collateral challenge may be available for an inherent lack of jurisdiction or an apparent nullity, but not merely for a disputed factual predicate requiring investigation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 21 and 39 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a permission granted under Section 21 is presumed valid until set aside through an appropriate challenge. Collateral challenge concerns whether a decision exists in law, not whether it should be invalidated on the merits. It may be available for an inherent lack of jurisdiction or a proceeding visibly branded as invalid, but not where disputed facts require evidentiary investigation. The test of jurisdiction over the subject matter is whether the tribunal can decide the case at all, not whether it may issue a particular order while deciding it. The Court commented on Subhash Kumar Lata v. R.C. Chhiba and explained S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, J.R. Vohra v. Indian Export House Pvt. Ltd., Shiv Chander Kapoor v. Amar Bose, and Yamuna Maloo v. Anand Swarup; it also referred to Joginder Kumar Butan v. R.P. Oberoi.

rule.if: limited_tenancy_enforcement_proceeding and permission_granted_by_competent_body and permission_has_presumptive_validity and challenge_depends_on_disputed_facts and not inherent_jurisdictional_defect and not apparent_nullity

predicates.limited_tenancy_enforcement_proceeding: The proceeding seeks enforcement of a permission for a limited tenancy after the permitted period has ended.
predicates.permission_granted_by_competent_body: The permission was granted by a body competent to decide the type of matter before it.
predicates.permission_has_presumptive_validity: The permission has not been set aside in proceedings brought to challenge its validity.
predicates.challenge_depends_on_disputed_facts: The challenge depends on deciding disputed facts that require investigation or evidence.
predicates.inherent_jurisdictional_defect: The body lacked inherent authority to decide the type of case before it.
predicates.apparent_nullity: The decision is visibly invalid on its face.

issues.definition: In enforcement of a limited-tenancy permission, a collateral challenge is unavailable when the permission remains presumptively valid and the challenge turns on disputed facts, unless the decision suffers from an inherent jurisdictional defect or is facially invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Calling a transaction a fraud on the statute does not create a distinct remedy from the remedy for fraud that vitiates a limited-tenancy permission.
material_facts: The occupants characterized the alleged suppression of an earlier tenancy as a fraud on the statute.
The dispute concerned whether the limited-tenancy permission could be attacked as invalid in the subsequent possession proceedings.
issues.conclusion: Fraud on the statute is a figurative description of a colourable transaction intended to evade statutory provisions and does not, for purposes of choosing a remedy, differ from fraud that vitiates the permission.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “fraud on the statute” describes a colourable transaction intended to evade statutory provisions; it does not create a separate remedial category from fraud as a ground for vitiating a permission. The Court considered the challenge in light of its principles governing collateral attacks on permission under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

predicates.limited_tenancy_permission_dispute: The parties dispute the validity of permission for a limited tenancy.
predicates.alleged_evasion_is_described_as_fraud_on: A party alleges that a colourable transaction was used to evade statutory requirements and describes it as fraud on the statute.

issues.definition: In a dispute over limited-tenancy permission, describing an alleged evasive transaction as fraud on the statute does not create a remedy distinct from the ordinary remedy for fraud.

issues.legal_issue: Successive permissions for limited tenancies to the same tenant do not, without more, invalidate a later permission.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the validity of permission for a limited tenancy.
The Court addressed the contention that successive grants of limited-tenancy permission could be invalid merely because they were successive.
issues.conclusion: Successive grants of permission to let premises to the same tenant for limited periods do not, by themselves and without more, vitiate a later grant.
issues.legal_principle: A later permission for a limited tenancy is not invalid solely because permissions have been granted successively to the same tenant. The Court relied on Dhanvanti v. D.D. Gupta and observed that successive grants share, in one sense, the characteristics of a post-facto grant.

predicates.limited_tenancy_permission_dispute: The validity of permission for a limited tenancy is disputed.
predicates.successive_permissions_to_same_tenant: More than one limited-tenancy permission has been granted successively for the same tenant.
predicates.no_additional_invalidating_circumstance: No circumstance beyond the successive grants is shown to invalidate the later permission.

issues.definition: When permissions for limited tenancies are granted successively to the same tenant, succession alone does not invalidate the later permission.
